topic: When a word competes with a color
headline_fact: Naming an ink color and reading a word are different tasks.
summary: This lesson separates an illustrative experience, a proposed explanation, and a reported finding.
did_you_know: The task instruction matters when interpreting a response.
core_mechanics: An instructed response can compete with another available response.
why_it_matters: A measured task difference does not establish a personal trait.

in_depth_breakdown.real_world_application: Assess what a task actually measures before interpreting its outcome.

learning_takeaways: Separate the task, the finding, and the interpretation.

visual_suggestions.cover: An editorial illustration of printed color swatches on a desk, with one person considering a response. No words, letters, numbers, labels or brain imagery. Keep the left third quiet for a headline and the subject in the central 60 percent.

share_text: Start with the task. Then ask what the evidence actually supports.

sources.title: J. Ridley Stroop (1935): Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions

psychology_lesson.question: What happens when a word and its ink color disagree?
psychology_lesson.learning_goal: Distinguish an everyday illustration from a measured research finding.

opening_scenario.title: Imagine this small conflict
opening_scenario.situation: In this illustrative scene, a card says “red” but its letters are blue. The instruction is to name the ink color.
opening_scenario.question: Which feature should guide the response?

prediction.prompt: Consider the instruction before opening the explanation.
prediction.reveal: The instructed answer is the ink color.
prediction.explanation: This is a thought exercise, not a timed assessment or a personality score.

big_idea.name: Competing responses
big_idea.explanation: One stimulus offers more than one possible response. The instruction identifies which response is relevant.

explanation_steps.title: Identify the task
explanation_steps.explanation: Name the ink color rather than the written word.

explanation_steps.title: Separate the available responses
explanation_steps.explanation: The written color name and the ink provide different information.

explanation_steps.title: Ask what was measured
explanation_steps.explanation: A timing comparison concerns performance on a defined task, not a complete account of a person.

diagram.title: Keep the task and interpretation separate
diagram.caption: A conceptual map of the example. It contains no measured values.
diagram.description: Read the stimulus, task instruction, and response as separate parts of the situation.
limitations: This map does not measure a mental process or show a brain pathway.

nodes.label: Stimulus
nodes.detail: A written word and its ink color.

nodes.label: Response
nodes.detail: The answer given for this task.

edges.relationship: Consider the instruction when interpreting the stimulus.
Assess the response against the stated task.

worked_example.title: Interpret a hesitation
worked_example.situation: Imagine a person pausing before answering. This is an illustrative case, not a reported participant.
reasoning_steps: Avoid inferring a stable trait from one answer.
worked_example.outcome: The pause alone does not identify its explanation.
worked_example.interpretation: A useful next question concerns how the task was designed and measured.

alternative_explanations.title: An unclear instruction
alternative_explanations.explanation: In the illustrative case, misunderstanding the instruction is another possibility.
alternative_explanations.how_to_distinguish: Check that the person understands the task before interpreting the response.

evidence.title: The original color-naming comparison
evidence.finding: In Experiment 2, color naming took longer for conflicting color words than for color squares.
evidence.interpretation: This supports a task-specific interference finding. It does not identify an individual’s personality.

study_notes.method: Participants named ink colors in two conditions, with task order balanced.
limitations: The participant group and task constrain the conclusions.

statistics.label: Color-square condition: reported mean
statistics.interpretation: A group result for the reported task, not a predicted time for this reader.

statistics.label: Conflicting-word condition: reported mean
statistics.interpretation: Compare within the reported design; do not treat this as a personal benchmark.

replication.summary: This sample lesson cites the original report and does not assess repeat-study evidence.

populations: The cited report concerns its student participants.
contexts: The reported conditions use timed color naming.
limitations: Do not generalize a brief demonstration to every reading situation.
Do not use this activity to label a person.
uncertainties: The illustration does not determine the cause of any individual response.

practical_application.suggestion: Ask what a task actually measures
practical_application.reasoning: Separate the instruction, the measured result, and the interpretation before drawing a conclusion.
practical_application.limitations: This is a reasoning habit, not a promise of improved performance.

key_terms.definition: Competition that affects performance on a task.
A statement about what was observed, without settling every causal explanation.

deeper_detail.title: A finding is not a complete explanation
deeper_detail.explanation: The measured difference and an explanation of that difference answer separate questions. Compare the design with the claim.

knowledge_checks.question: Which feature does the illustrative task ask the person to name?
Does one hesitation establish a personality trait?
knowledge_checks.explanation: The reported task and the interpretation must stay separate.

takeaways: Keep a reported result separate from its interpretation.
Apply conclusions within their stated limits.
